newsitem.title: UK: Stg, dollar seen favoured as Buba and Bonn Clash.
newsitem.headline: Stg, dollar seen favoured as Buba and Bonn Clash.

text.p: Currency traders are diving for cover as the Bundesbank and Bonn cross swords about the credibility of plans to get Germany's fiscal house in order in time for European economic and monetary union.
And the safest havens are those which have the least to do with the single currency project -- the dollar and sterling.
"The Bundesbank's attack on a desperate government taking desperate measures has upped the stakes in a dramatic way," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London.
"But given the situation of what this means for EMU and the European crosses is far from clear, the key is to get the hell out of continental Europe, and buy dollars and sterling."
Sterling jumped to 2.7875/85 marks by 0743 GMT from 2.7720/30 late Wednesday in Europe, while dollar/mark climbed to 1.7029/34 from 1.6902/07.
The mark crosses, by contrast, were broadly steady. The mark was quoted at 3.3793/95 French francs and 992.00/30 Italian lire against 3.3817/22 and 992.11/11 late on Wednesday.

A delay to the launch of EMU would trigger demand for marks at the expense of currencies such as the lira and the peseta as it would prevent the mark being subsumed into a potentially weaker and less stable currency.
But there is nothing as yet to indicate that the Bundesbank's objections to the German government's plan to revalue its assets would derail EMU, analysts said.
The parliamentary group leaders of Germany's coalition government have said they will push ahead with their plans regardless.
Still, now that the Bundesbank has dropped its mask of diplomacy, traders are faced with the prospect of a protracted squabble about how strictly to interpret the Maastricht criteria for EMU entry.

"There's a lot of stuff frothing around about EMU and convergence criteria but the market is convinced that something will happen on January 1, 1999," said Gerry Celaya, an analyst at American Express Bank. "This means people are either sitting on their hands or buying a few dollars as a hedge."
The traditional bolt hole of the Swiss franc has attracted fewer traders, given the Swiss National Bank's repeated pledge to combat any rebound in the franc.
The SNB has flooded the money market with liquidity in the past week, forcing short rates lower and keeping talk alive of a cut in the discount rate from 1 percent.
This has enhanced the attraction of sterling for those looking for safety but wishing to remain in Europe.

The opt-out from EMU which the UK negotiated in the Maastricht treaty, and the government's pledge to hold a referendum on whether to join monetary union makes the UK an unlikely EMU candidate in traders eyes.

Add to that expectations UK interest rates are headed higher and the fact that benchmark 10-year UK bonds offer a bigger premium over bunds than the bonds of most other EU countries, and traders are more than happy to buy pounds in preference to marks or other continental European currencies.
"Opting out is looking like the best option right now," said Norfield at ABN Amro.
